title: The Day the Wind Stopped
hookLine: baby Hanuman leaps for the sun, Indra strikes him down, and the wind god stops: every creature chokes
carry: pranayama tends breath as a sacred gift
tomorrow: speech, mind or breath: who really holds the body up?

lines: A BABY JUMPS FOR THE SUN.
cards: A baby wakes up hungry. Above him, the rising sun glows red, and he thinks it's a fruit. So he jumps for it.
This is Hanuman, son of Vayu, the wind, and in the Ramayana's telling he leaps right up into the sky.
Indra, king of the gods, alarmed, strikes him with his thunderbolt, and the child falls onto a mountain, his jaw broken. Then his father does something terrible and quiet. Vayu stops.
Today, the day the wind stopped blowing, and what it teaches about breath.

teach.b: Vayu, grieving, takes his son into a cave and holds still. And because the wind is also the breath in every body, everything chokes.

Creatures can't breathe, the text says; their bodies go stiff like wood; the gods themselves are in distress. They run to Brahma, the creator, who comes to the cave and revives the child, and the wind moves again.
Then the gods, one by one, give Hanuman boons, and the Ramayana ties his name to that broken jaw, hanu. Here is the teaching, named plainly. In Hindu thought, breath isn't just air.
Vayu is a god, and prana, breath, is life itself, given to every body. That's why yoga treats breath with care.

Patanjali's Yoga Sutras make breath practice, pranayama, one of yoga's eight limbs, and describe it simply: the breath out, the breath in and the pause, watched by place, by time and by number, becomes long and fine.
That's a description, not a promise. It doesn't say a pattern heals illness, and it gives no count of seconds.
So this week, every claim about breath gets one of three labels: the text says, tradition says, or a doctor decides. One plain safety line, because breath work isn't neutral.
Anyone with a heart or lung condition, anyone pregnant, anyone who gets dizzy or anxious with breath exercises keeps to easy natural breathing and asks a doctor before any holding of the breath.
Today's practice holds nothing. It only watches, the way you'd look after a gift.

how: Hanuman's leap at the sun is told to Hindu children in Ramayana retellings, and some yoga teachers who follow Patanjali have students watch the breath before regulating it, adapting or skipping breath-holding for students with health conditions.

o: a breath pattern that cures whatever ails the body
plain air, with nothing sacred in it
breath as Vayu's gift, watched with care, not forced

games.q: the wind and the breath — tap the pairs.
p: breath practice, one of yoga's eight limbs

s: in the Ramayana, when Vayu stopped, beings couldn't breathe
the wind is the breath in every body. the gods ran to Brahma, and the child was revived.
the Yoga Sutra gives a breathing pattern that heals illness
it describes breath under attention becoming long and fine. no cure, no count of seconds.
in Hindu thought, breath is just air
Vayu is a god, and prana is life itself, given to every body.

games.q: you're Vayu. your baby son has been struck down by Indra's thunderbolt. what does the wind do?
o: stop moving, and take the child into a cave.
keep blowing as if nothing happened.
games.why: Vayu holds still, and every creature chokes. the gods run to Brahma, the child lives, and the wind moves again: breath is the life of everything.

practice: Let the breath do whatever it's doing, and watch it by place, where it's felt most, then by time, whether the in-breath runs longer than the out-breath, then by number, counting a few breaths from one to five, without changing anything.
If it grows longer and finer on its own, notice that; if it doesn't, that's an honest result too. If you pray, let each out-breath be a small thanks to the One who gives it.

wordCard.voice: The breath again. When Vayu stood still, every creature choked; in the Yoga Sutras, breath watched by place, time and number becomes long and fine. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit vayu: wind, and the wind god, Hanuman's father. the same word names the breaths that move in the body.

carryVoice: Your line: pranayama tends breath as a sacred gift. The text says, tradition says, a doctor decides. That's today, done.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Uttara Kanda 35–36 (the infant Hanuman leaps at the sun; Indra's thunderbolt breaks his jaw; Vayu withdraws into a cave and beings cannot breathe; the gods go to Brahma, who revives the child; the gods' boons; the name from hanu)
Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda 66 (Jambavan retells Hanuman's birth and leap at the sun)
Yoga Sutras 2.29 (the eight limbs, pranayama among them)
Yoga Sutras 2.49 (pranayama follows posture: a pause in the flow of in-breath and out-breath)
Yoga Sutras 2.50 (the outward, inward and held movement, observed by place, time and number, becomes long and subtle)
